title: Coarctation of the Aorta
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A congenital narrowing of the aorta, usually just after the ductus, causing upper‑body hypertension, weak lower pulses and a characteristic murmur. Early recognition prevents heart failure and aneurysm.

sections.p: Coarctation is a segmental narrowing of the aorta, most often juxtaductal. It is a structural heart defect that can be isolated or part of a syndrome.
b: Juxtaductal narrowing causes pressure overload of the left ventricle

t.b: Measure upper and lower limb BP; a delay >0.5 s or a difference >20 mmHg suggests coarctation.
Shows a high‑velocity jet across the narrowed segment; confirms location and severity.
May show rib notching from collaterals and a small left heart border.
Provides detailed anatomy when surgery is planned; used if echocardiography is inconclusive.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the pressure gradient across the coarctation and the presence of collaterals.
b: Grade I: <20 mmHg gradient, minimal collaterals
Grade II: 20–40 mmHg, moderate collaterals
Grade III: >40 mmHg, marked collaterals and symptoms

sections.p: The primary cause is a congenital narrowing; associated conditions are often syndromic.
b: Turner syndrome (most common syndromic association)
Ehlers–Danlos, Loeys–Dietz, and other connective tissue disorders
Isolated congenital defect

sections.p: Symptoms vary with age and severity.
b: Infants: poor feeding, tachypnoea, cardiomegaly
Children: hypertension, weak femoral pulses, rib notching
Adolescents/Adults: headache, claudication, back pain

sections.p: Choose tests based on availability and clinical urgency.

t.b: Detects upper‑lower limb gradient; a delay >0.5 s is a red flag.
First‑line imaging; shows gradient, ventricular size, and associated lesions.
Rib notching suggests long‑standing collaterals; useful when echo is unavailable.
Rule out associated syndromes (e.g., thyroid function for Turner).

sections.p: Early complications can be fatal if untreated.
b: Heart failure from LV hypertrophy
Aneurysm of the aorta or intercostal arteries
Hypertensive crisis

sections.p: Treat the narrowing and support the heart.
b: Surgical repair (end-to-end anastomosis or patch) is definitive
Percutaneous stenting in selected cases

t.b: Reduce afterload and LV wall stress; first choice in acute hypertension.
Used after surgery to control BP; avoid in pregnancy.
Consider if aneurysm is present to prevent thrombus.

sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on BP control and surveillance for aneurysm.
b: Annual BP checks
Echocardiography every 1–2 years
Lifestyle advice: salt restriction, exercise

sections.p: Conditions that mimic the clinical picture.
b: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy – similar LV hypertrophy but no limb BP gradient
Rheumatic heart disease – can cause murmur but not limb BP delay
Aortic dissection – sudden onset pain, but imaging differentiates

sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal early.
b: Chest X‑ray may be normal in mild cases
Echocardiography can miss a very small coarctation if the probe is not angled correctly

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypertension with headache or visual changes

faq.q: How do you differentiate coarctation from hypertension due to other causes?
faq.a: Look for a delay in femoral pulses and a gradient between upper and lower limb BP; imaging confirms the narrowing.

faq.q: What is the first imaging modality in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Echocardiography is the first choice; if unavailable, a chest X‑ray and limb BP comparison can raise suspicion.

faq.q: Can coarctation be treated medically alone?
faq.a: Medical therapy controls symptoms but does not correct the structural defect; definitive repair is required for cure.

exam: What bedside sign would you look for to suspect coarctation? — Weak femoral pulses and a delay >0.5 s in radio‑femoral pulse transmission.
Which imaging study is most definitive for surgical planning? — CT or MR angiography of the aorta.

Why is a beta‑blocker preferred in acute hypertensive crisis in a child with coarctation? — It reduces afterload and LV wall stress without causing significant vasodilation that could worsen the gradient.
What complication is most feared if the coarctation is left untreated into adulthood? — Aortic aneurysm or dissection.
How would you explain the ‘rib notching’ seen on chest X‑ray? — Collateral intercostal arteries erode the inferior margin of ribs over time.
In a child with Turner syndrome, why is routine screening for coarctation important? — Turner syndrome has a high incidence of post‑ductal coarctation, often asymptomatic until adolescence.
